issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere under its second-appeal jurisdiction with concurrent findings of fact when the lower courts misapply the law, place the burden of proof on the wrong party, or materially misread or ignore evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court dismissed the challenge to the settlement deed.
The first appellate court overlooked the age stated in the deed and concluded that the executant’s age had not been proved.
Neither court properly considered the absence of testimony from the deed’s witnesses or the person who identified the executant’s thumb impression.
The courts placed on the plaintiffs the burden of proving the deed’s validity.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering because the lower courts’ findings resulted from legal errors and disregard of material evidence; the limits on interference with concurrent factual findings did not prevent it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure ordinarily limits interference with concurrent factual findings, but permits it after formulation of a substantial question of law where the lower courts misdirect themselves on a question of law or burden of proof. Under Yadarao Dajiba Shrawane v. Nanilal Harakchand Shah, [2002] 6 SCC 404, interference may be warranted where findings rest on misinterpretation of documentary evidence, inadmissible evidence, ignored material evidence, or ignored admissions or concessions. Under Neelakantan v. Mallika Begum, [2002] 2 SCC 440, findings may be set aside if they lack a basis in legal evidence, misread evidence, or suffer from a materially prejudicial legal infirmity. Chandra Bhan v. Pamma Bai, [2002] 9 SCC 565, and Sakhahari Parwatrao Karahale v. Bhimashankar Parwatrao Karahale, [2002] 9 SCC 608, concerned materially different factual circumstances and did not bar interference here.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and (wrong_party_bore_legal_burden or material_evidence_was_ignored or documentary_evidence_was_misread)

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from lower-court findings.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual conclusion.
predicates.wrong_party_bore_legal_burden: The lower courts assigned the burden of proof to a party who did not bear it.
predicates.material_evidence_was_ignored: The lower courts failed to consider evidence material to the dispute.
predicates.documentary_evidence_was_misread: The lower courts misunderstood or misread documentary evidence.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges concurrent factual findings, interference is permissible if the lower courts wrongly assigned the burden of proof, ignored material evidence, or misread documentary evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming a benefit under a challenged deed must prove its due execution, and a person in active confidence who benefits from a transaction must establish its fairness and bona fides; where the executant is old, infirm, or illiterate, proof must establish a mental act as well as a physical act of execution.
material_facts: The deed purported to transfer property from an executant described in it as 106 years old to the defendant and his minor son.
The executant was alleged to be illiterate, paralytic, ailing, and in an impaired physical and mental condition.
The deed recorded that the executant was affected by old age and ailments.
No deed witness was examined to prove execution, and no witness was examined to establish that the executant placed the thumb impression attributed to him.
The defendant relied on the deed, while the lower courts wrongly placed on the plaintiffs the burden of proving its validity.
issues.conclusion: The burden to prove the deed’s validity and execution rested on the defendant claiming under it; the High Court was justified in holding the deed void and invalid on the record before it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 111 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 places the burden of proving good faith on a person who is in a position of active confidence in a transaction with another. A person who obtains a benefit under a voluntary transaction must establish its fairness and bona fides when a confidential or fiduciary relationship gives rise to a presumption of influence. Clause (3) of Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 reflects the corresponding principle concerning undue influence. Independently, a person claiming rights under a document must prove due execution. The protection discussed in Mst. Kharbuja Kuer v. Jang Bahadur Rai, AIR 1963 SC 1203, for a pardahnashin woman applies by analogy to an old, infirm, or illiterate person unable to understand the document: proof must establish the executant’s mental act, not merely the physical act of making a mark.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenges_beneficial_deed and claimant_relies_on_deed and (execution_is_unproved or (executant_was_vulnerable and informed_execution_is_unproved) or active_confidence_relationship)

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_beneficial_deed: A civil suit challenges the validity of a deed that confers a benefit.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_deed: A party relies on the deed to claim a benefit or rights under it.
predicates.execution_is_unproved: The party relying on the deed has not established that the executant duly executed it.
predicates.executant_was_vulnerable: The executant was old, infirm, illiterate, or otherwise unable to understand the document unaided.
predicates.informed_execution_is_unproved: The party relying on the deed has not established that the executant understood and freely performed the transaction.
predicates.active_confidence_relationship: The beneficiary stood in a confidential or fiduciary relationship that placed the beneficiary in active confidence over the executant.

issues.definition: A party relying on a beneficial deed must prove due execution, and must also prove informed, fair dealing when the executant was vulnerable or the beneficiary occupied a position of active confidence.
